summary: Children, a spouse and parents have a reserved share (iryubun) of one half of the estate, or one third if only parents survive; since 2019 it is a money claim. A foreign national's estate is governed by their national law. Japan has a Trust Act and the general incorporated foundation, but has not joined the Hague Trusts Convention.
reserved_share: Spouse, children and their descendants: one half of the estate; parents or other ascendants only: one third; multiplied by each heir's statutory share (Civil Code art. 1042). Siblings have none. Since 2019 the claim is for money (art. 1046).
foreign_law_note: Act on General Rules of Application of Laws art. 36: succession is governed by the law of the deceased's nationality at death, so a foreign national resident in Japan keeps their national law (subject to renvoi and public policy). This is a default rule, not a free choice. Japanese real estate may still raise lex situs questions.
trust_note: Not on the HCCH status table. The Trust Act (Act 108 of 2006) allows ordinary, testamentary and family trusts; for tax a trust is generally looked through to the beneficiary, and the Inheritance Tax Act art. 9-2 treats the creation of a trust for a beneficiary as a gift or bequest. The General Incorporated Associations and Foundations Act (Act 48 of 2006) allows a general incorporated foundation with ¥3 million of assets for any lawful purpose, but Inheritance Tax Act art. 66(4) can tax it as an individual if it reduces family tax.
open_questions: I did not retrieve the Japanese Law Translation text; confirm arts. 1042, 1046 and the article numbers of the two Acts there.
